items.title: Vampire Survivors Review: Evolution, Adventure, and the Birth of a Genre
items.summary: Vampire Survivors has been evolving for five years, and after enjoying Legacy of the Bloodmoon, it felt right to take stock.
items.content:
Vampire Survivors has a lot to answer for. This site, for example, probably doesn’t exist without it. Along with Hades, this genre-making bullet heaven has been one of my go-to games because of how regularly it provides an abundance of the things that I enjoy about gaming: novelty, surprise, and interesting decision-making.

Vampire Survivors and games like it have sometimes drawn derision from certain quarters. I’m never one to yuck someone’s yum, but I’ve seen plenty of that around. I want this review to be a counterpoint to that sentiment. I think bullet heavens are excellent alternatives to action-roguelites that often require manual dexterity and a degree of genuine skill. Because the gameplay is kept simple here, you’re able to focus on decision-making.

I think my favourite thing about Vampire Survivors is the theory crafting, which is where it is today thanks to years of updates and iteration that have added to the pot. The base game was a complete experience at launch, and since then, the game has been updated with several massive expansions and chunky, free content patches.

There are so many different characters to learn, and each one has a subtle configuration to work around as you level it up. Each one has a starting weapon, which you can evolve as you collect the experience points dropped by the enemies you kill with your automated attack. There are also several slots for additional weapons and items, and your success over the course of a run will depend entirely on how you get your build set up.

The single-stick controls and the simplicity of the core gameplay might be a limitation in some aspects, but it has also allowed for rapid iteration and a constant churn of engaging new content, as well as fresh ways to experience the same material in remixed ways.

Adventures are a good case in point. These more focused campaigns allow you to recapture that early game feel once more, as new characters and in-game quests give fresh life to old pixels. Not only are there impactful game modifiers to tinker with, but it’s a great way of familiarising yourself with the game’s vast cast of characters.

If anybody happens to read this, I’ll follow up with a deeper dive into the DLC rather than getting into it here. There’s a risk that we’ll get lost in the weeds, so let’s focus on the post-launch content more generally. The new DLC, Legacy of the Bloodmoon, is a good example of what poncle is doing with content, and it’s fresh in mind as I’ve been playing it in the evenings.

Bloodmoon adds a whole bunch of new characters and weapons. While they are fundamentally more of the same, there’s pleasing variety, and you can mix and match them with existing tools to find new ways to complete a run.

The injection of new content adds more depth to an already deep experience. The fact that poncle’s in-house DLCs cost a solitary unit of money – still a favourite detail of mine – means that the overall package is insanely good value for money.

When it comes to crossover content, there are already three major collaborations that you can enjoy. Among Us, Contra, and Castlevania. That last one – Ode to Castlevania – is my favourite of the three, as Vampire Survivors clearly owes a debt to the artists at Konami, and that particular DLC feels like a perfect fit for this IP.

These expansions cost a little more than the in-house DLCs, but not much more, and they offer lots of thematic ways to experience Vampire Survivors anew. In fact, I think the overall level of fan service here is actually pretty good.

My kids were drawn to the Among Us expansion, Emergency Meeting ; Contra is all about the guns; and I love a bit of gothic monster-whipping. Ultimately, I think you’re going to get more out of each DLC if you like the original IP that it’s based upon. And I think that probably holds true on future projects, including Jujutsu Kaisen Rumble: Survivaton and Warhammer Survivors (Auroch Digital), which are both upcoming spin-offs built on the same core bullet heaven concept.

Another standout feature that needs a shoutout is the soundtrack. The devs have gone to a lot of trouble to make sure that the OST is varied, and if you like classic arcade music and chiptunes, I think you’ll like this, too. New music is constantly being added to the mix, making this a very cool selling point if you enjoy this sort of music.

The graphics are the final piece of the puzzle, and if you’re a pixel art nerd like me, you’ll enjoy the overall aesthetic. It’s not a neglected part of the game, but it is kept simple on purpose. It’s a trade-off I’m happy to make for the sake of greater gameplay diversity. Having said all that, if you’re not charmed by what you see, nothing I say is going to change your mind, and that’s ok, too.

items.summary: Vampire Survivors: Legacy of the Bloodmoon is a fantastic expansion that brings in great new characters and weapons for only $1.
items.content:

Vampire Survivors is a phenomenon that doesn’t stop giving. Even now, after hundreds and hundreds of hours I put into it, I feel like the gameplay never gets old and there’s always something new to discover. Part of that comes from the continuous updates and expansions that the game gets, and the new expansion is another reason to dive back in and enjoy the game all over again.

Last week, the game had a new expansion release called Legacy of the Bloodmoon , which came out of nowhere to me. It’s essentially the alternative to its Legacy of the Moonspell expansion, focusing instead on the villains. And just like all of the other expansions, it comes with new content across the board with new characters, weapons, and a brand new big stage.

I was quite pleased with the new characters, and felt the weapons were very unique compared to what we’ve seen before. From Malice’s Scarlet Needle that pierce his enemies and stops them in their tracks for quite some time, to Sargon’s three Fire spells that can combine into a crazy powerhouse with flames everywhere, it felt like there was something to enjoy when I’m unlocking all 16+ new weapons.

And each of the characters have a unique effect that makes them worth playing. Most of these effects are triggered in certain situations, like when you’re attacked, your health is at critical, or you revive. One of the characters even get the new passive weapon slot every time you revive past the first time, which is pretty awesome if you can get multiple revives. There are 12 characters in total to unlock, and some of them surprised me. One of them even costs 540,000 gold coins, which shocked me at first until I saw who I was actually going to play as.

The map also has a great balance of size, power up to fine, and bosses to kill. Like the other expansions, all the characters can generally be unlocked by completing different objectives on this map, and I quite enjoyed myself doing so. There’s a lot to experience, and it felt great to discover it for myself.

There’s even a brand new Adventure to enjoy. I can’t say I spend a lot of time in these contained versions of the game, but it is no doubt interesting and cool to have. There are eight chapters to play through, which tells a little story about the relevant characters in this expansion. It’s not something I found myself playing a lot of, but it’s a nice little extra.

And at the end of the day, what makes this such an amazing deal is that it's extremely cheap. The entire expansion is just $1, making it extremely cheap to add more content to the game. This falls in line with the prices of their other expansions, with the most expensive one being $4 MSRP, and it makes it so worthwhile. The pricing for the game and it’s expansions have always been extremely competitive, and it’s hard not to justify getting more characters, weapons, a new stage, some fantastic new music, and a brand new Adventure, for the cost.

If you enjoy Vampire Survivors and like great games to play on the Steam Deck, do yourself a favor and pick up this expansion.

Vampire Survivors: Legacy of the Bloodmoon is $1 on Steam. To celebrate the expansion, the base game and its other DLC are all 25% off.

items.title: Vampire Survivors Meets Spelunky Is My Newest Obsession
items.summary: Messhof's latest turns bullet heaven into a neat and chaotic platformer
items.content:
Blood Dungeon Roguelike Spelunkey Vampire Survivors

Blood Dungeon is a chaotic bullet-heaven platformer that will have you climbing up the walls, literally. Your character sticks to everything in this platformer. It takes the irresistible formula of Vampire Survivors and applies it to 2D dungeon crawling for a frenetic and challenging arcade mix that makes you work hard for your rewards rather than letting you just sit back as optimally managed RNG runs its course. For that reason, it might be my favorite one of these yet.

The latest indie game from Messhof, best known for Nidhogg , Fly Wrench , and last year’s Wheel World , Blood Dungeon ‘s pitch is fairly straightforward. You pick one of nine unlockable characters, embark on one of six unlockable dungeons, and juggle over 100 auto-firing upgrades to fight over 100 enemies to complete over 100 quests. Instead of just hopping from one surface to the next, you can crawl along walls and ceilings, hugging them like a caterpillar on cocaine. Each arena has its own theme and design—one takes you underwater while another is an endless well—but the enemies inside and the locations of certain upgrades are randomized for each run.

You get upgrades by collecting blood from the stuff you kill. It might give you a laser beam or a sword that spins around you. Rare charms might let you freeze enemies or zombify them. As you play and die, more stuff gets unlocked, and the builds start to get more exotic. Basketball weapons will bounce between the walls. Spiderweb guns will shoot webs you can then use to climb in midair. Instead of just balancing upgrades that scale with overall survivability, you’re considering which upgrades might make it easier to navigate 2D mazes and dodge the increasing waves of enemies that populate them.

Blood Dungeon is in the lo-fi doodle art style of designer Mark Essen’s previous solo projects like Nidhogg . The enemies and characters exude a combination of whimsy and irreverence. One character is nude with censor bars across their body and moves only by doing cartwheels. A machine gun icon looks very much like a dick and balls. And one of the bosses, a giant worm, is right out of Nidhogg . The soundtrack by Thomas Hoey, who also composed the music for Wheel World , fills each dungeon with its own unique, trance-like vibe. All of this was neat enough, but I wasn’t prepared for just how deeply Blood Dungeon would sink its pixelated meat hooks into me.

Vampire Survivors games are great at exploiting that feeling that just getting to the next upgrade will solve all your problems, especially once you die and it’s game over. Just one more run to get a luckier drop and all will be well. Otherwise you don’t really do much in the game itself other than the buildcrafting equivalent of counting cards at a casino. Some Survivors -likes have tried to solve for that by giving you more agency over avoiding the hazards flying around the screen, but none that I’m aware of have injected what is essentially Diablo -style RNG into the classic, Mario Bros. -esque 2D platformer as well as Blood Dungeon .

While Messhof has leaned on comparisons to Spelunky and the way that you’re constantly scrolling through levels in search of new secrets and unlockables when asked about Blood Dungeon ‘s inspirations and influences, I think there’s a bit of Pac-Man DNA in Blood Dungeon as well. The mazes you’re exploring have an urgency as if the walls are constantly closing in. Sit still and you’ll be got. Move in the wrong direction and you might get trapped in a dead end. It’s only after repeated playthroughs that you start to memorize the larger structure of the arenas and are able to begin making split-second decisions about which tunnel to follow where and what your plan-B and plan-C exits might be along the way when things fall apart.

This is the part of the game that’s kept me coming back. Dying and grinding to unlock new secrets is cool. Getting your favorite upgrade—in my case the laser beam—three times in a row to power it up into a path-clearing nuke is a lot of fun. But the cat-and-mouse chase as my knowledge of the dungeons grows makes me feel like less of a dopamine-drip-fed pawn in the whole affair. I’m only five hours into Blood Dungeon , but unlike Ball X Pit , which made me feel vaguely gross about wanting to continue playing, Blood Dungeon feels like an arcade cabinet I want to spend all week saving my quarters up for until I’ve mastered what it has to offer.

items.title: Vampire Survivors Gets Bloodier and Raunchier In Blood Dungeon
items.summary: Messhof's latest is a Microsoft Paint fever dream
items.content:
on Google Preferred Source Google News Link copied to clipboard By Giovanni Colantonio Published Aug 24, 2026, 12:00 PM EDT Reviews Messhof's latest is a Microsoft Paint fever dream

Image: Messhof Add Us Add on Google Preferred Source Google News Like Like follow Follow followed Followed Thread Log in Here is a fact-based summary of the story contents: Try something different: Show me the facts Explain it like I’m 5 Give me a lighthearted recap Here’s a two-word video game review for you: Blood Dungeon . That’s it. That’s the review.

No, really, what more do you need me to say? It’s a video game called Blood Dungeon . Bless developer Messhof, the studio behind Nidhogg and Wheel World , for giving its latest game a title that tells you exactly what you’re getting with this lo-fi Vampire Survivors riff upfront. It’s like seeing a store-brand cereal called Sugar Balls. No confusion about what’s in that box! As it says on the tin, Blood Dungeon is about as lowbrow as video games get — and that’s exactly what I ordered. It’s a proudly crude roguelike built for a generation raised on Adult Swim. Sometimes, you just crave something that dares to be stupid.

Blood Dungeon is, essentially, Vampire Survivors if it were remade by a 12-year-old in Microsoft Paint. Poncle’s retro pixel art has been replaced by misshapen doodles colored in with magic markers. Splotchy blue birds and disembodied hands roam around 2D arenas that look like they were made from texture stamps. It’s like opening your kid’s school notebook and having the horrifying realization that they are not, in fact, paying attention in math class. That lends Blood Dungeon a sense of gleeful immaturity that I was ready to embrace immediately.

The gameplay follows all the basic rules of Vampire Survivors. You pick a misfit character (my favorite is a nude dude who moves by cartwheeling, the Skinja) who has their own starting weapon and perk, move around a level as your weapon auto-fires at enemies, and pick up new upgrades as you collect blood to level up. Blood Dungeon is a DPS arms race, even more than Vampire Survivors, with an emphasis on getting your baseline power up to snuff over crafting tricky builds. That can make the decision-making feel a little limited, but there’s still room for aha moments. My best run to date had me focusing on upgrades that cut down my weapon cooldowns (reducing them when I was at full health and standing in a spawned circle) until I was killing bosses before they even appeared on-screen. Get stuffed, Bone Dragon!

Blood Dungeon is a high-score chase first and foremost.

If you don’t enjoy outfitting a tiny hero with shotguns and rotating swords until they slowly transform into a mobile murder machine, Blood Dungeon isn’t likely to change your mind — but it might . The most noticeable difference is that Blood Dungeon is a 2D platformer, so you have to slink around obstacles while dodging swarms of enemies. It’s a slight tweak, but one that gives the action a jungle gym energy. You’ll clamber up chain fences, hop over spikes, and swim through water tunnels in a handful of arenas that play with terrain in different ways. It’s a more active variant of the formula that gives you something to do aside from moving your joystick and choosing between three upgrades.

The more meaningful change, though, is the pace of a run. A game of Vampire Survivors is a bit of a commitment. You can’t claim victory unless you survive 15 to 30 minutes, leading to slow-building runs where you spend a lot of time standing around until the tension starts to ramp up. Sometimes you make it to the 20-minute mark only to learn that your build just doesn’t cut it, leading to a fast death. Blood Dungeon escalates much quicker and has multi-tiered victories, which makes bad runs feel like less of a waste of time. The ultimate goal of a level (or at least the way to properly “beat” it and earn a crown) is to survive long enough to beat three bosses, but you’ll unlock new stages so long as you can beat the first one. Every achievement after that is a matter of chasing unlocks and bragging rights.

Image: Messhof The inclusion of online leaderboards signals that Blood Dungeon is a high-score chase first and foremost. Beating a level is fun and all, but obliterating your friends’ bone count and rubbing it in their face is the real reward. I got competitive — okay, toxic — during my few weeks with it, sending screenshots of my scores to friends who were also reviewing it to taunt them. (In my defense, I beat their asses so goddamn bad, dude.)

Also, did I mention that the name of the game is fucking Blood Dungeon ? That’s pretty crucial.

Even though I’ve played plenty of games that are similar to Vampire Survivors , like Megabonk and Brotato , the quicker pace of Blood Dungeon finally helped me understand why I’m so drawn to the format. Vampire Survivors feels like a modern arcade game. I can imagine walking up to a cabinet with a handful of quarters and trying to see how far I can get in a run, as I still do with Ms. Pac-Man anytime I find it in the wild. Plenty of roguelikes fit that description, but Vampire Survivors stands apart by being squarely focused on a streamlined style of play that’s easy to learn and hard to master. It subtracts where so many of its peers pile more systems on top of the ones popular games have established; Vampire Survivors is more a continuation of Asteroids than Hades .

Blood Dungeon fully leans into that philosophy. I love firing it up for a single run, rather than compulsively sitting with it for hours on end. I set a new high with a build that involves a basketball and two Desert Eagles, and then turn it off and return the next time I’m bored to see if any of my sorry ass friends have managed to beat me. (Fat chance!) It only took me around six hours to properly clear each level and nab over 50% of the unlocks. Great! Now it sits permanently installed on my Steam Deck like Space Invaders on a multicab. I know I’ll get the urge to fire it up on a lazy Sunday.

Image: Messhof That’s not to say that it’s an elevated take on Vampire Survivors that revolutionizes the “Bullet heaven” subgenre. Blood Dungeon is a shallow riff on the formula. There are a lot of toys to experiment with, but there’s not too much depth. There are only a few levels in the game currently, and at least one of them is a dud. (Trying to fend off enemies underwater while grabbing oxygen bubbles to stay alive? No thanks!) It can feel like a quick prototype for a bigger idea, a Hail Mary thrown by Messhof to nab a hit in the wake of its more ambitious Wheel World .

It will either find its audience or it won’t. And its audience is people who see the name Blood Dungeon and think, “haha, hell yeah.” And brother, as someone who is squarely in that group of Neanderthals, let me tell you that it’s hitting the spot. Shotgun shoot 13 shells at skeleton head. Big sword go spin. Ha ha. Blood good, want more blood.

items.title: How Vampire Survivors became Vampire Crawlers: Six lessons from building a game based on another developer's IP
items.summary: Nosebleed Interactive's Andreas Firnigl on crafting a spin-off of Poncle's smash hit: pub prototypes, shared rules, last-minute changes and more
items.content:
Nosebleed Interactive's Andreas Firnigl on crafting a spin-off of Poncle's smash hit: pub prototypes, shared rules, last-minute changes and more

Image credit: Nosebleed Interactive/Poncle Academy by Andreas Firnigl CEO, Nosebleed Interactive Published on Aug. 10, 2026, 3:19 p.m. Follow Nosebleed Interactive Andreas Firnigl started his career as a tester on Big Mutha Truckers, way back on Gamecube. He founded Nosebleed Interactive almost 15 years ago as CEO and creative director.

In 2023, an old contact I had worked with 15 years ago – and who is now at Poncle – came to us with the amazing opportunity to collaborate on a Vampire Survivors spin-off.

Luca Galante, the creator of Vampire Survivors, had come up with the idea for a card game spin-off and had already developed an early prototype, but Poncle wanted an external studio to help turn it into a complete game. So lead designer Luke Wintflint and I worked with Luca and Poncle to evolve that idea into what became Vampire Crawlers.

After 15 years making games and working with other studios, Nosebleed Interactive has learnt a lot about how to treat someone else's IP and how to collaborate with external partners. We learnt even more on Crawlers, and I want to share some key lessons that you can take away and apply at your own studio.

Naturally, understanding the IP you are working on is vital. Yet it's even more important to demonstrate to the client that you understand it.

I've put a stupid amount of hours into Vampire Survivors in order to understand all the little nuances and tics that most people won't notice. This kind of intense playing helps you to understand what is changeable and what is not. Some things will be fundamental to the experience and will have to be incorporated, while others are things that, frankly, players don't care about all that much. Knowing what can and can't be changed is a sign you are working on something you understand, rather than doing a half-arsed superficial imitation.

The fundamentals of Vampire Crawlers came together very quickly. A pen and paper version that we played in the pub during the early days of development was surprisingly close to the final game. However, in those early months, we paid less attention to the IP and were instead focused on adding content, throwing in random stuff willy-nilly as a placeholder. We knew it would be quick and easy to fix later on, and knew enough about the IP to do it right – but Poncle didn't.

We had the bones of a great game, but it wasn't clear to Poncle that we had a good Vampire Survivors game. So we downed tools on everything else and focused on fixing that – making sure all the names were right, matching up how stats would transfer from Survivors to Crawlers, and so on. As soon as Poncle saw the next build, they gave us the green light.

In short, do that work of understanding your partner's IP – but make sure you show them you have that understanding, too.

Fans of the IP will naturally be interested in playing your new game, but you also need to make sure it works for people who don't know the original title. This is why it's important to get feedback from people who haven't played the IP at all.

There were a couple of people at Nosebleed who hadn't played Vampire Survivors, and rather than encouraging them to try the game, we asked them to avoid playing it at all. Having some folks on the team who are coming in clean, as it were, was a real help to balance the onboarding, which is so important in this kind of game. Relying too much on knowledge of the existing IP could make it less attractive to new players.

Your partner is working with you because you have something to bring to the table (there's certainly a lot of Nosebleed's DNA in Vampire Crawlers). So lean into your strengths – but be humble. Be prepared to learn from how your partner works, and what works for their IP.

Before Crawlers, we'd just come off Arcade Paradise, where the density of every pixel had to be exactly correct. Would Poncle do that? No.

items.title: Vampire Survivors' new spin-off has hooked me (and Combolands could, too)
items.summary: Plus: Krafton up, Xbox down, Roblox down, CCP left... and a PowerWash dev comment from 2021 that was suddenly relevant this week.
items.content:
Stephen Totilo May 02, 2026 30 1 3 Share Vampire Crawlers. Screenshot: poncle, Nosebleed Interactive I think I really liked 2022 indie breakout Vampire Survivors . But I have long wondered if the game just made me think I liked it. Playing it felt great. Maybe too great?

In Vampire Survivors, you’re a hero warrior guy or a magician lady or maybe even an old man with some repellent garlic. From a top-down perspective, you see your hero swarmed by skeletons, bats and very annoying preying mantis-like creatures (but no vampires, of course). You cannot manually attack your foes. The attacking is automatic, and you just move. As enemies are killed for you, they drop blue gems. Collecting them fills a bar. Filling the bar unlocks a selection of upgrades. Those upgrades can make your attacks more powerful or more frequent. Maybe they give you a second attack, perhaps some spinning books to supplement your whip or your lightning.

If you’ve played it, you know how smoothly Vampire Survivors draws you in and how tightly it keeps you from doing anything but play it. It chirps with slot-machine sounds. It fires off virtual fireworks as you crack open a treasure chest. That progress bar keeps filling up, and the rewards keep on coming. Where once you were weak, soon you’re strong.

Did I like Vampire Survivors? Or did I just like how much it felt like a constant celebration of mindless, near-endless winning?

(The one thing I was sure was genuinely good about the game was that my kids, my wife and I could easily play it together. That was indisputably wonderful.)

My too-many hours enraptured by Vampire Survivors led me to approach its first big spin-off, April’s Vampire Crawlers , with great caution.

Crawlers is played solo in a first-person perspective, one turn at a time, as your warrior man or magician lady dungeon-crawls through forests, bridges, libraries. I presume there eventually is, an actual dungeon but I haven’t spoiled myself. Each region is filled with enemies and the occasional treasure chest.

As I dove in, I heard the familiar slot machine sound effects and saw a progress bar that kept filling up as I killed skeletons, bats and very annoying preying mantis-like creatures (but, so far, no vampires).

Here we go again, I thought. Another seductively mindless game that I better be ready to tear myself from. Actually, I was wrong about the mindlessness.

I knew that combat in Vampire Crawlers is not automatic. Each attack or item is represented as a card, and battles are a matter of randomly drawing cards from a tiny deck into your hand, then playing them, registering their effects on the enemies, discarding them, earning more cards for your deck, shuffling and playing through it again. With each hand, you can choose which cards to play or play all of them in a single button press. I mistakenly thought the latter was the preferred action. After all, Vampire Survivors didn’t even want me to press a button to attack. Surely the gameplay joke of Crawlers is that I should just play all of the cards in my hand at once?

I was initially playing Crawlers by spamming the all-cards-at-once option and the action was feeling as mindless as Survivors. But, as would be obvious with any other card-based game, Vampire Crawlers players are best served by choosing the right card to play each time. The key to the combat system involves card combos. The game’s attack cards, hero cards and item cards cost different amounts of magical mana points to play. The potency of those cards increases if you play card in the order of their mana cost. For example, you’d ideally first play a card that costs zero mana, then a card that costs one, then a two card, to keep the combo going. If you’re clever, you’ll work in wild cards, maybe turn a card’s value negative. Perhaps there are other tricks I’ve yet to discover to keep the combo going.

Once this combo system clicked, I realized that the gameplay in Vampire Crawlers is meant to be thoughtful, not mindless. When playing, I need to think about how I’m building my deck to increase the chance that my randomly drawn hand will contain cards I can combo consecutively. As I’ve been playing, I’ve needed to think about which new cards to grab, which ones to trash, all to build the most potent deck. I need to be strategic. If Vampire Survivors was a slot machine, maybe this is at least poker or craps.

As with Vampire Survivors, Crawlers is proving hard to quit. This time, I don’t feel as guilty when the minutes (or hours) stack up.

A demo for Combolands was quietly released last month. It’s fascinating.

items.title: Vampire Crawlers Is A Vampire Survivors That's Better For Your Heart Rate
items.summary: The followup game to Vampire Survivors keeps the hook but loses some of the chaos
items.content:
I wasn’t exactly a model fan of Vampire Survivors , Poncle’s 2022 reverse bullet hell. I absolutely loved its strangely Zen blend of chaos and strategy and mindlessness, but I never got great at the strategy part. I’m not by nature a min-maxxer, and I tend to get a bit overwhelmed when a game has too many stats, instead picking some power or combo I like and sticking with it even if it isn’t ideal. So far, followup game Vampire Crawlers is giving me the same things I loved and the same things I’m less passionate about, but with a slower pace that’s helping me get more into the strategy mindset.

Vampire Crawlers (full title: Vampire Crawlers: The Turbo Wildcard From Vampire Survivors , and out now for PC and consoles) is developed with a studio called Nosebleed Interactive. You still traverse areas like a forest and a library, and you’re still levelling up all the time. But it turns Vampire Survivors into a first-person, deck-based dungeon crawler: each turn, you have a certain amount of mana to spend playing cards that can do damage, give you armor, boost your other cards, and more. As you play, you get new cards or the opportunity to tinker with your current cards to make them more powerful.

The key thing to think about here is combos, in particular the order you play your cards in. If you play them in ascending order of mana cost (0, 1, 2, etc), you’ll run up a streak that boosts the next costliest card. It’s not always the move–sometimes a nasty boss required me to ignore the combo in favor of piling on my armor, or I was me about a turn and just couldn’t resist a powerful card even if it broke my combo–but it was always on my mind as I chose my plays. This can feel a little rote at times, or at least in the early game where I still am, but I also felt like it helped guide my decision-making a little more than my long-running natural tendency to just start clicking instead of taking my time.

Like Vampire Survivors , there’s a meta-game, though this time it’s laid out in an interface charmingly stylized like a village. You can spend the gold you earn during runs on permanent power-ups and on characters with unique abilities. There’s a world of things to unlock and combine and tinker with, and I get the sense this will all become vital as the difficulty ramps up.

You could argue there’s something a little disappointing there, an encouragement to replay and grind for coins and levels that could start to drag when combined with Vampire Crawlers ’ slower pace. In Survivors , the chaos of the game distracted me from all this–every level, even if I’d seen it all before, was fast and exciting, so it never felt like I was just doing the same thing over and over, even though I was arguably doing less than I do in Crawlers . But so far, I’m finding it a good balance: Even if I’m playing a level again, I’m still excited about which cards I’ll get and which order I’ll play them in and what I can do to boost a hand. It feels like there’s a little more to do in each turn of each run, combined with the primordially satisfying flood of damage and XP. And there’s still the pleasantly thoughtless allure of “one more battle” and “one more level” that made Survivors such a particular mix of complexity and ease.

Similar to Balatro , I think one of the core appeals of Survivors and now Crawlers is sort of “breaking” the game–getting so strong and pulling down such big combos that the whole thing becomes an overpowered exercise in absurdity. It’s a strange kind of mastery when compared to other games that require more personal skill, and it’s one I find both appealing and a little hollow. I’m not sure I’ll ever have the kind of brain that will get me there before other games pull me away–the ability to develop an encyclopedic understanding of Crawlers’ trinkets and stats and combos–but so far it feels more achievable for me in Crawlers than in Survivors given its slower pace.

Vampire Crawlers keeps the core hook and essential structure of Survivors while doing its own unique thing with its own particular rhythm. I can see it joining the rotation of games I play when it’s a little too soon to go to bed, but without the adrenaline rush of Survivors that made it not great for actually going to bed. I spent the morning with it and am excited to see more of what it has to offer, even if I’m probably not the kind of person who will ever find my way to its end.

items.title: The Vampire Survivors developer is opening studios and making over 15 projects
items.summary: Poncle is opening studios in Japan and Italy as Vampire Survivors sails past 27 million players
items.content:
Playback speed × Share post Share post at current time Share from 0:00 0:00 / Generate transcript A transcript unlocks clips, previews, and editing. 16 2 The Vampire Survivors developer is opening studios and making over 15 projects Poncle is opening studios in Japan and Italy as Vampire Survivors sails past 27 million players Christopher Dring Apr 22, 2026 16 2 Share Transcript The Game Business is Live in Los Angeles on Monday, June 8, where we will be interviewing video game royalty Laura Miele, Jason Rubin and Matthew Ball live on stage. Tickets are available now.

Listen now on Apple , Spotify or YouTube In This Edition, Poncle’s Matteo Sapio on: - Vampire Survivors spin-offs and tie-ins - Opening studios in Japan and Italy - Working on over 15 projects

During last week’s London Game Festival, I spoke with Matteo Sapio, the chief strategy officer at Vampires Survivors developer Poncle.

We were speaking in front of a live audience, and it was one of the most revealing interviews I’ve done since launching The Game Business . During out chat, Sapio announced:

That Vampire Survivors has now surpassed 27 million players

It has over 15 projects in active development (and even more in earlier stages)

It is licensing out its engine to other brands and studios to build ‘Survivors’ games based on popular IP

It has paused its third-party publishing plans

“Vampire Survivors came from a solo developer,” Sapio explains. “It was Luca Galante, who made a game for him and his friends. Vampire Survivors exploded, and in two or three months, it sold more than one million copies. Luca’s yachts are video games. So instead of buying a yacht, he made the Emerald Beyond DLC [for Vampire Survivors] with Square Enix, which we released for free. Things grew organically from there.”

For more surprising developer interviews, sign-up to The Game Business today

First, there are spin-offs to Vampire Survivors. This includes the deck-building card battler Vampire Crawlers, which is out this week.

“We [are using] the famous Vampire Survivors IP to experiment in new genres,” Sapio tells us. “We love card games, but we are not very good at card games. They’re complicated. So, we made the game that we wanted to play.”

Vampire Crawlers is out this week Second, Poncle is working on original IP. Sapio says the company is currently developing two entirely original properties.

And third , there will be a range of new ‘Survivors’ games based on other IP. These are Vampire Survivors-like games set in other universes. Some will be developed by Poncle, whereas others – such as the upcoming Warhammer Survivors – are in collaboration with other studios.

items.title: Looking Back (and Forward) at the Success of Vampire Survivors
items.summary: Exploring bullet heaven's beginnings and future with a hit indie four years later
items.content:
Exploring bullet heaven's beginnings and future with a hit indie four years later

Becoming a SUPERJUMP member is free — save stories to your library and pick up reading on any device.

It has been about four years since the release of Vampire Survivors (VS) blew up the indie space and created the “bullet-heaven” genre. Developers have been chasing after the game's success ever since. With the latest DLC inspired by Castlevania, I jumped back into the game to see if the gameplay still works today in light of the many games I’ve played since. Surprisingly, it does, and has lessons to teach the games that are trying to vie for the crown.

At this point, I don’t think I need to explain what Vampire Survivors is , and I want to skip to where it is today.

Vampire Survivors has come a long way in terms of its design. The original map was simply an empty field that stretched on infinitely. Now there are multiple maps, multiple characters, secrets, additional systems, and this doesn’t even include the latest map.

Perhaps the most surprising thing about going back to VS today is that it still plays as one of the faster bullet heaven games on the market. When I last played, it had the option to increase the in-game speed so that 30 minutes became 20. Now you can do it even faster, going down to 15 minutes — allowing someone to experience a full run quicker than any other bullet heaven out there.

This gets at one of the biggest issues I have with a lot of other games: the developers keep messing up the speed. I’ve lost count of the number of these games where the very first run is slooooow — your character is slow, bullets are slow, enemies are slow; the entire game feels slow. I’ve had to institute a new rule — if I’m falling asleep before ten minutes are up in your game, I will end the run early.

For the games in which I do manage to get to the end of a run, through death or completion, I’m surprised to find that I’ve unlocked nothing at all. If you’re going to do a game like this, there must be consistent upgrades to drip-feed progression. I’ve lost count of the number of games where the first upgrade takes multiple winning runs to unlock.

It’s this slowness that betrays a lot of the bullet heavens compared to Vampire Survivors. I'm willing to bet that these games have nowhere near the amount of content that VS has at this point, so slowing down progression keeps them from running out of things for the player to do. However, it’s that amount of content and the consistent rewards that keep someone engaged with VS. If I want to make progress in the game, I can go after a character challenge, weapon unlock, map unlock, or just go for gold that I’m going to be using for more meta unlocks.

There is a puzzle to playing and mastering the many different items, tarot cards, and characters that isn’t present in the other games. It’s that next level of understanding that provides a lot of the replayability in Vampire Survivors — yes, you survived a run, now how do you break it?

To that point, let’s talk about the newest map. The Castlevania/Symphony of the Night DLC is the closest fans have gotten to a celebration of the series in a long time, and definitely not from Konami themselves. Featuring remixed versions of popular songs, a buffet of characters from the series, the largest map to date in the game, and many different secrets to find.

Each “adventure” map adds more features and elevates the original formula, but this one is the most expansive to date. It contains a lot more unlockable characters, bonus areas, and more nods to the entire Castlevania franchise.

What makes this one of the best bullet heaven experiences is the sheer number of secrets and places to explore, which does something I haven’t seen in any other bullet heaven to date — it makes me want more time to explore.

There are so many new weapons, combinations, and permanent upgrades that you can unlock on the map that, despite Vampire Survivors being the first bullet heaven game to blow up, it still feels like one of the most progressive takes on the genre. It’s those details that keep Vampire Survivors on top of the subgenre and is the bar that other games must clear if they want to have any chance at exceeding the standard set by the king of the genre.
